title: How Gutter and Drainage Failures Push Water Into a Home | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: Why the same wall gets wet every monsoon. How roof runoff, scuppers, grading and site drainage move water into Phoenix area homes, and what to look for.
h1: How Gutter & Site Drainage Failures Push Water Into a Home
intro: It is the same corner every time. A storm rolls through, and a day or two later the baseboard in that one room feels soft again, or the paint on the garage wall bubbles up in the same spot it did last August. You painted over it. You had someone look at the roof and they said the roof was fine. Maybe it dried out on its own and you stopped thinking about it until the next time. What makes this kind of problem hard to sit with is not the damage itself, it is not knowing why it keeps choosing that spot. Water does not behave randomly, but it also does not announce its route. It can enter twenty feet from where it shows up, travel along a framing member or the top of a slab, and surface somewhere that makes no sense. So you are left patching a symptom, year after year, with the quiet sense that you are missing something you should have figured out by now.

sections.heading: Recurring wet spots usually mean water is being delivered, not leaking
sections.body:
There is a useful distinction between a leak and a delivery problem. A leak is a hole: a failed pipe, a cracked tile, a bad flashing joint. A delivery problem is when something outside the house is concentrating a large volume of water at one point on the building, and the building was never designed to hold back that much water in that one place. Almost no residential wall assembly is waterproof. Walls are water resistant, and they shed water on the assumption that gravity and the site are carrying most of it away. Take that assumption away and the wall starts losing.

That is why the same corner floods every year while the rest of the house stays dry. The rest of the house is not better built. It just is not being hit with a hundred gallons off a roof plane in fifteen minutes. On a flat or low slope roof, which is common across Phoenix, Mesa, Chandler and Scottsdale, one scupper or one downspout can be handling runoff from a very large area of roof. Everything that lands up there is funneled to a few small openings. When one of those openings is blocked, undersized, or discharging in the wrong place, the water still has to go somewhere.

sections.heading: The specific failure points that put water into a wall
sections.body: Most drainage related intrusion traces back to a short list of physical problems. Walking the perimeter during or right after a storm, when you can actually see where water is going, tells you more than any dry inspection.

cards.heading: Blocked or overflowing scuppers
cards.body: Flat and low slope roofs drain through scuppers or roof drains at the parapet. Palo verde litter, gravel from the roof surface, a bird nest, or a dislodged strainer can dam one off. When it backs up, water rises behind the parapet and finds the wall cap, the scupper flashing seam, or the joint where the parapet meets the roof deck. That water then runs down inside the wall cavity and shows up on an interior ceiling or upper wall, often on the opposite side from where you would expect.

cards.heading: Downspouts that discharge at the foundation
cards.body: A downspout that dumps straight onto dirt or a narrow gravel strip at the base of the wall is concentrating roof runoff into a small patch of soil right where you least want it. That soil saturates, the water spreads laterally under the slab edge or against the stem wall, and it wicks in. Splash blocks help less than people think. Extending the discharge several feet away from the building, onto a hard surface that slopes away, is what actually changes the outcome.

cards.heading: Negative or flattened grading
cards.body: Soil should fall away from the house for the first several feet. Over years it settles, gets built up by landscape rock added on top of old rock, or gets raised by new planter beds and pavers. Once the grade is flat or tilted back toward the wall, storm water pools against the foundation. In yards with caliche or heavily compacted soil, which is much of the Valley, that water does not percolate down. It sits and looks for a path sideways.

cards.heading: Hardscape and stucco below grade
cards.body: A patio, walkway or driveway poured tight against the house often ends up higher than the weep screed, the metal strip at the bottom of the stucco that lets trapped water drain out. When landscaping, pavers or added concrete cover that screed, the stucco has no exit. The wall assembly holds water, the bottom plate stays damp, and drywall and baseboard rot from the inside out with no visible exterior source at all.

cards.heading: Overflowing or detached gutters
cards.body: Gutters that are pitched wrong, packed with debris, or pulled loose at the fascia will sheet water directly down the wall behind them. That constant wetting rots fascia and soffit and can track back into the eave and along the top plate. On homes with gutters draining to a single corner, a clog turns the whole run into a waterfall at one spot.

cards.heading: Yard drains and area drains that no longer drain
cards.body: Courtyards, side yards and sunken patios often rely on a catch basin piped out to the street or an alley. Those lines silt up, get root intruded, or were never sloped correctly. When the basin stops accepting water, a courtyard becomes a shallow pond with a door threshold on one side of it. This is a frequent source of interior flooding in walled or courtyard style homes in Gilbert, Queen Creek and San Tan Valley.

sections.heading: How to trace water back to its actual entry point
sections.body:
Water travels down and sideways along whatever is easiest: the top of a slab, the bottom plate, a stud face, a pipe or a wire penetration. So the wet drywall is the end of the story, not the beginning. A few things worth checking before assuming the roof or a plumbing line is at fault.

Timing is the strongest clue. Damage that appears only after rain, and never in the dry months, points at the exterior and the site rather than at supply plumbing. Damage that appears in July with no rain, or that stays wet continuously, points at a pipe or an appliance line.

Height matters too. Staining that starts at the floor and climbs up the drywall a few inches is water arriving from below or at slab level, which is the signature of grading, hardscape, or a buried drain. Staining that starts high and runs down is roof, scupper, parapet or eave related.

Look for efflorescence, the white chalky mineral bloom on block, stucco or concrete. That is dissolved salt left behind by water that moved through masonry and evaporated. It marks a path water has taken repeatedly. Rust on the bottom of a metal door frame, or a threshold that has lifted, tells you standing water reached that spot. Soft or spongy baseboard on one wall while the adjacent wall is fine narrows the entry point considerably.

Also pay attention to what is behind the wall. Dark spotting on drywall, a musty odor that gets stronger when the AC kicks on, or paint that keeps blistering in the same place after repainting all suggest the cavity has stayed damp between events rather than drying out fully. Drywall, insulation and framing that go through repeated wet and dry cycles degrade even when nothing ever looks dramatic.

sections.heading: Fixing the water and fixing the damage are two different jobs
sections.body: Correcting drainage stops the next event. It does not undo what already happened inside the wall. If water has been arriving at the same place across multiple seasons, the material behind the paint has been holding moisture, and drying it properly means opening the assembly, measuring the moisture in the framing and the substrate, and drying to a target rather than to how it looks. Setting a fan in the room does not reach a wet bottom plate inside a wall cavity. The reverse is also true. Replacing drywall and baseboard without changing where the water goes just resets the clock on the same problem. That is the loop a lot of homeowners get stuck in, and it is why the repair keeps feeling like it did not take. faqs.q: Why does the same wall get wet every year even after I repaint it?
faqs.a: Because paint is not stopping water, it is covering the evidence. If the wetting happens only after storms, something outside is delivering concentrated water to that spot: a downspout discharging at the foundation, a blocked scupper, grading that slopes back toward the house, or hardscape covering the weep screed at the base of the stucco. Until that delivery path changes, the wall will keep getting wet on the same schedule.

faqs.q: How can I tell if it is a drainage problem or a plumbing leak?
faqs.a: Timing is the clearest test. Drainage related intrusion shows up during or shortly after rain and dries back out between storms. Plumbing leaks do not care about the weather, so damage that appears or worsens during a dry stretch, or that never fully dries, is more likely a supply line, drain line or appliance connection. Height helps too: damage starting at the floor and moving up usually means water arriving at slab level from outside.

faqs.q: Is a splash block enough to protect the foundation under a downspout?
faqs.a: Usually not on its own. A splash block breaks the force of the falling water but still leaves it within a foot or so of the wall, where it soaks into soil that is already against the foundation. Carrying the discharge farther out, onto a surface that slopes away from the house, does far more. In yards with caliche or compacted soil that drains slowly, distance from the building matters even more because the water will not soak down quickly.

faqs.q: There is no visible damage yet, just a musty smell after it rains. Is that worth looking into?
faqs.a: Yes. Odor that appears after rain and fades in dry weather usually means a cavity is taking on moisture and holding it long enough for growth to start, even though the drywall surface still looks intact. Damage inside a wall assembly is almost always further along than what shows on the paint. Checking it while it is still a smell is a much smaller project than checking it after the drywall fails.
